title: Why People Obey the Law
text:
In the mid 1980s the psychologist Tom Tyler asked a basic question: why do people follow the law? The usual answer was fear of punishment. Tyler suspected that something else mattered as much: whether people saw the authorities as legitimate.

He and his team interviewed about 1,500 randomly chosen residents of Chicago by telephone, asking about their views of the police and courts and about how often they broke everyday laws such as speeding, littering or shoplifting. Many had recently dealt with the police or courts themselves, for example after a traffic stop or a call for help. About a year later, many were interviewed again.

The results surprised many legal scholars. Whether people obeyed the law depended strongly on whether they saw the authorities as legitimate, more than on how likely they thought they were to be caught. And when people judged their own encounters with police or judges, what shaped their views most was not whether they won or lost, but whether the process had been fair: whether they had a chance to explain themselves, whether the officials were neutral and honest, and whether they were treated with dignity.
lesson: People accept even unwelcome decisions when they feel the process was fair and they were heard with respect. Fair procedures build the authority that force cannot.
source: Tyler, T. R. (1990). Why People Obey the Law. Yale University Press.
